activity.text: Welcome to the latest edition of The Innovation Continuum. I recently had the privilege of speaking on the main stage at NEXT Pharma Summit in Dubrovnik about something I've been thinking about for years: Why do so many digital transformations fail—even when we have the right strategy, the right technology, and the right people? Research suggests around 70% of digital transformation initiatives fail to achieve their intended outcomes. And around 67% of well-formulated strategies fail due to poor execution. So if it's not strategy... and it's not technology... where is the problem? It sits in the middle. Between strategy and execution. Where global meets local. Where Commercial meets Medical. Where ambition is meant to become action. This is where organisations actually work. And this is where transformation breaks. 💡 Read this edition if you're interested in why transformation fails in the middle, and what it takes to fix it. #DigitalTransformation #Pharma #Leadership #TheInnovationContinuum ...more

What if healthcare isn't missing data… but missing signals? We’re very good at capturing clinical events: diagnoses, treatments, interventions. But we’re often far less effective at capturing context, lived experience, and how health is actually experienced over time. And when those signals aren’t captured meaningfully, something bigger happens: People stop feeling heard. Trust erodes. Important insights are lost. During a recent conversation on the FearlessHer podcast, we explored why healthcare systems often struggle to reflect the reality of women’s experiences — particularly when symptoms are complex, interconnected, and evolve over time. One of the themes I kept coming back to was this: If we don’t analyse differences, we won’t see them- and if we don’t see them, we won’t design for them. As we build more AI-enabled and data-driven healthcare systems, representation alone isn’t enough. We need to intentionally design for insight. That means moving beyond episodic snapshots toward longitudinal understanding. Beyond isolated clinical events toward lived experience. Because the best technology in the world still won’t capture the right data if we lose sight of the humans at the centre. Thank you Rachael Onwona Dentaa and FearlessHer for creating such a thoughtful conversation. You can watch / listen to our conversation here ↓ https://lnkd.in/eX-9e8S3 Disclaimer: The views expressed are my own and do not reflect those of Ferring Pharmaceuticals. ...more

After two days at NEXT Pharma Summit Pharma, I've been reflecting on the conversations that stayed with me most. Three themes particularly resonated: 🔵 Strategic foresight vs forecasting Pharma is very good at forecasting—modelling, planning, predicting what's most likely to happen. But foresight is different. It's about building the organisational muscle to explore multiple possible futures, challenge assumptions, spot emerging signals, and make better decisions today because we're more prepared for tomorrow. That feels increasingly important in a world where AI, patient behaviour, healthcare systems and access models are all evolving at pace. 🔵 The changing nature of treatment decisions Treatment decisions are no longer shaped by one stakeholder or one moment in time. Clinical evidence still matters deeply, but evidence alone doesn't guarantee access. Decisions are increasingly shaped by reimbursement, payer dynamics, affordability, real-world value, clinical pathways and patient expectations. We have to think much more systemically about value. Not just: have we developed an innovative medicine? But: can patients actually access it? Can healthcare systems afford and adopt it? 🔵 Always-on HCP engagement I particularly enjoyed the session Iria Gala was part of, because it brought to life something I am personally very passionate about: moving on from campaign-based engagement towards continuous, insight-led, AI-enabled experiences that respond to what HCPs actually need in the moment. HCPs aren't living in our campaign cycles. Patients aren't waiting for our launch plans. Healthcare decisions are happening continuously. The question is no longer only how we reach people. It's how we listen, learn, and respond in ways that are relevant, timely and trusted. Thank you to NEXT Pharma for creating the space for these conversations. I’ll be sharing more thoughts in next week’s newsletter on the messy middle of transformation - and why this translation challenge matters so much if we want to move from fragmented innovation activity to meaningful impact. A special thank you as well to the other speakers and panellists whose sessions helped shape these reflections — including Travis K. , Mirkka Schaller, PhD , Agathe Acchiardo , Sarah Clark -Pfister, Dan Cohen , Delphine Caroff , Serena Planera and Arantxa Mugica Goicoechea . Serena and Arantxa’s session before my keynote really brought the “missing middle” to life in a practical way - a great reminder that transformation often gets hardest in the space between the ambition on the slide deck and the reality of execution. And a huge thank you to Dario Safaric , Lucija Glavina , Antonija Zadravec , Petra Safaric and the wider NEXT Pharma team for creating such a thoughtful, energising and well-curated event. There were so many thoughtful conversations across the two days, and I left with plenty to keep thinking about. ...more

Tomorrow I’ll be speaking at NEXT Pharma Summit 2026 in Dubrovnik. After 24+ years across life sciences, technology, and transformation, one pattern keeps repeating: We don’t have a technology problem. We have a translation problem. I’ll be delivering a keynote on the main stage at 11.20am “From Strategy to Impact: Fixing the Missing Middle in Pharma’s Digital Transformation.” Because while we’ve made real progress in digital, AI, and omnichannel - very little of it consistently translates into impact at scale. Not due to lack of investment. Not due to lack of ambition. But because what sits between strategy and execution - the middle - is often undefined, fragmented, or overlooked. I’ll be sharing a perspective on: ➡️ Why transformation breaks between global strategy and local execution ➡️ The role of operating models, governance, and ways of working in enabling (or blocking) progress ➡️ Why AI and data won’t deliver value without fundamental shifts in how work gets done ➡️ What it takes to move from isolated pilots to embedded, repeatable capability If you’re attending NEXT Pharma in Dubrovnik (19–20 May), I’d love to connect. #NEXTPharma Disclaimer: The views expressed are my own and do not reflect those of Ferring Pharmaceuticals. ...more

I’m excited to be joining the main stage at NEXT Pharma Summit in Dubrovnik next week for a panel exploring a question many pharma organisations are still grappling with: Are field roles truly evolving — or are we creating an identity crisis? MSLs, reps, hybrid roles, digital engagement specialists… Across the industry, we continue redesigning field models around new channels, technologies, and organisational structures. But perhaps the more important question is: What do healthcare professionals actually need from us? Because when every interaction is measured by activity rather than value… when touchpoints multiply but meaningful engagement does not… and when we digitise field models without fundamentally redesigning the engagement model itself… …we risk optimising for the wrong outcomes. I’m looking forward to discussing this alongside Carlos Sosa (Almirall), Olivier Burgaud (Servier), and Mehrnaz Campbell (Cheemia), as we explore what field roles should become in an increasingly omnichannel world — and why the future of engagement is less about channels and titles, and more about relevance, trust, orchestration, and experience. 📍 NEXT Pharma Summit | Dubrovnik 📅 19–20 May 🎤 Main Stage Panel | 12:00–12:20 And if you’re attending, I’ll also be speaking earlier that morning on: “From Strategy to Impact: Fixing the Missing Middle in Pharma’s Digital Transformation” 🕚 11:20am Would love to connect with others attending the event. #NEXTPharma #DigitalTransformation #Omnichannel #Pharma #CustomerEngagement #MedicalAffairs ...more

There’s something very humbling about putting a group of professionals—used to operating in their own lanes—in front of a violin. No slides. No titles. No hierarchy. Just people. At our recent Digital, Commercial Excellence & Data & Analytics F2F, we took part in an Orquestra Na Hora session - learning to play as an orchestra in real time. And it wasn’t really about music. It was about humans. Because transformation doesn’t fail because of technology. It fails because of behaviour. No one in that room had ever played a violin before. Success didn’t come from expertise. It came from something far more fundamental: ➡️ Being open to trying something completely new ➡️ Being willing to be led by someone new ➡️ Trusting the process (even when it felt uncomfortable) ➡️ Feeling safe enough to get it wrong in order to get it right That’s culture. And without it, no amount of digital, data, or AI will ever scale into real impact. We talk a lot about “orchestrated customer engagement” in pharma. But orchestration isn’t a capability you install. It’s a behaviour you build. And this is where transformation so often breaks. Not at the strategy level. Not at the technology level. But in the middle. The space where people, behaviours, and ways of working either come together… or don’t. 🔵 How well do we listen across teams? 🔵 Do we optimise for individual performance or collective outcomes? 🔵 Are we aligned on the same rhythm—or creating noise? Individually, we can all be strong. But transformation—real, sustainable transformation—only happens when people move together. That’s what turns strategy into impact. Here's my question: how much of your transformation budget goes to the technology - and how much goes to building the culture that determines whether anyone actually uses it? Thanks to the team for their input and making the day so enjoyable! Ljiljana Vucetic | Carla Santos | João Barata DISCLAIMER: The views expressed in this post are my own and do not reflect the views of Ferring Pharmaceuticals. ...more

I had the pleasure of joining the Harvard Medical School Senior Life Sciences Leaders Program last month as an industry speaker, and I genuinely enjoyed every single minute of it. We started the session the same way I often start conversations with my own teams: “What does digital transformation mean to you?” It’s a simple question, but you learn a lot from the answers. It gives you immediate insight into how people are thinking: → Their level of understanding → Their mindset and priorities → The role they believe they play in it → And often, where the disconnects are That question alone often explains why transformation is hard. There was a wide range of answers from the audience as expected. From "implementing new technology" to "fundamentally changing how we operate" to "something IT owns." That range itself was the point: if your organisation doesn't have a shared understanding of what you're trying to achieve, you're already starting from different places. From there, the discussion naturally moved into the realities of delivering digital transformation in life sciences: → Organisational readiness is often the biggest constraint - not the technology → Culture isn’t a “soft” topic; it’s the determining factor in whether transformation succeeds or stalls → And too often, digital is still approached as a set of tools, rather than a fundamental shift in how we work We also explored the role of AI. Where it’s already creating value, but also the responsibility we have to adopt it thoughtfully and intentionally. What made the session particularly valuable was the openness of the conversation. It was grounded in real experiences, challenges, and perspectives from across the industry. A big thank you to Kimberly Cremers, PharmD for facilitating such a great discussion and creating the space for a genuinely meaningful exchange. These are exactly the kinds of conversations we need more of if we want to move beyond ambition and into real impact. What does digital transformation mean to you? Genuinely curious to hear how people across the industry would answer. ...more

I have just completed a fantastic week of work experience at Charlie Bigham’s, and I would like to express my sincere gratitude to everyone who made it such a valuable and enjoyable experience. Throughout the week, I had the opportunity to gain first-hand insight into the finance function of a large manufacturing business. I was exposed to a wide range of areas, including accounts payable, accounts receivable, invoice processing, forecasting, and risk management, which helped me develop a much deeper understanding of how finance supports day-to-day operations and long-term decision-making within a business. One of the highlights of the week was independently researching and presenting a project on improving cash flow and exploring the use of AI within the business. This gave me the opportunity to apply analytical and presentation skills while receiving valuable feedback from experienced professionals. A special thank you to Nehal Kaura for providing me with this opportunity and making the experience possible. I am also incredibly grateful to Ryan Danison for taking the time to mentor and support me throughout the week. Ryan was exceptionally generous with his knowledge, ensuring I gained meaningful exposure to different aspects of the business and helping me understand the practical realities of working in finance. What stood out most was the positive and welcoming culture at Charlie Bigham’s. Everyone I met was approachable, supportive, and willing to share their expertise, creating an environment where I felt encouraged to ask questions and learn as much as possible. Thank you once again to everyone at Charlie Bigham’s for such an insightful and rewarding experience. I have learned a tremendous amount in a short period of time, and it has further strengthened my interest in finance and business. #WorkExperience #Finance #Business #Learning #ProfessionalDevelopment #CharlieBighams

I’m delighted to welcome Peter Wissing to Ferring Nordics as our new Country Sales Head for Denmark & Norway. Peter brings extensive leadership experience from the pharmaceutical industry, most recently from Organon and previously from MSD, where he held several commercial and market access leadership roles, including within fertility and women’s health. What stands out about Peter is his ability to build high-performing teams, foster strong collaboration, and deliver meaningful outcomes for patients and healthcare stakeholders. His experience and leadership will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our business across the Nordics.
